utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, with the last witness, you bar tabled the document 00974, a letter from Mr. Cetina. I'm informed that this document, which was assigned number D1770, was already in evidence as D1748.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Our apologies, Your Honour, may we vacate it in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1770 is vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you ready, Mr. Kay, to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. The witness is Mr. Vedris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could Mr. Vedris be escorted into the courtroom. No protective measures sought, and no objections from the Prosecution to admission into evidence of the 92 ter statement, which was filed on the -- I think the 4th of -- 10th of September, and the other Defence teams have not responded to the motion. Good morning, Mr. Vedris.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text was handed out to you by the Usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vedris. Please be seated. Mr. Kay. Mr. Vedris, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vedris.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, there is a screen on your right, and I'll ask for a document to come up onto that screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could 2D00736 be placed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You will see a statement in the Croatian language. And --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the front of that document, can you see your signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the document can be moved down on the page.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that a copy of your signature in a Croatian language version of a statement you gave to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at the last page of Mr. Vedris's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's the last page of the statement, and we can see the date of the 2nd of April, 2009. Did you sign that statement on that day, and is that your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: That's right, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And before signing that statement, did you read through it to check the document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was the information contained with that -- within that statement, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Vedris signed each page in between, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I was to ask you the same questions today as were asked when you made this statement, would the answers that you gave be the same as those contained within the statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I ask that this document be made a court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1772.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1772 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will give a short summary of the statement now for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, I'm going to summarize the statement for the Court record in a very short form, and then I will ask you a few extra questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour the statement of Mr. Vedris discloses that, in 1990, he was appointed by the Assembly of the city of Zagreb, the president of the Executive Council for that city, a function which later became statutorily renamed as being the position of the mayor of the city of Zagreb. Between 1990 and 1992, he was also president of the Crisis Staff for the city. As the Court will know from the evidence, that was a time of conflict within the states of the former Yugoslavia. From April of 1992, he was appointed as a minister without portfolio in the government of Croatia, responsible for urban living and the reorganisation of public administration. Later on in 1992, at the end of the year, he was appointed Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia for the economy. However, in March of 1993, after 100 days, he resigned from that post as Deputy Prime Minister and moved to being the position of the president of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce, whilst, at the same time, being a member of parliament. And Mr. Vedris continued with positions within public life, but also, in private life, formed his own international advisory company and more recently has been employed at the Faculty of Law at the University of Zagreb as a professor of economic policy. Mr. Vedris knows Mr. Cermak well. He was aware in autumn of 1991 when Mr. Cermak was appointed in the government of national unity to the position of being an assistant minister for defence with responsibility for logistics. The two of them cooperated together, because, as I have informed the Court, Mr. Vedris was concerned with the city of Zagreb and there was an infrastructural role for the city in relation to times of conflict and the needs for the defence of the state. Later on, in 1993, Mr. Cermak became a minister for economy, and at that time, Mr. Vedris, having resigned as Deputy Prime Minister for economy and moving to the Croatian Chamber of Commerce where he was the president, brought again the two into cooperation with each other, as they were both in two linked areas of responsibility. Later on, in 1993, Mr. Cermak resigned from his political position and returned to his private business interests. In August of 1995, Mr. Vedris, on the 5th, received a telephone call from Mr. Cermak, telling him he'd been appointed the commander of the Knin Garrison. The two of them, at that stage, were sharing office premises and had an association with each other through their business interested. Mr. Cermak informed Mr. Vedris that he was going to Knin because the president personally asked him to, to help organise civilian life for a short time. At that time, as they were sharing an office building together, when Mr. Cermak returned on occasions to Zagreb from Knin, he spoke about the work he was doing in the area. Mr. Cermak had to return to attend to business matters and discussed his work in Knin with Mr. Vedris, who had had his responsibilities as being the mayor of the city of Zagreb, and was aware of various infrastructural needs that had to be undertaken at that time. Your Honour, that's a brief summary of Mr. Vedris's statement to the Court, and with the Court's leave now, I will ask him some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, I'm going to ask you some personal questions about Mr. Cermak, first of all. It's correct from your statement - is it not? - that you've known him since the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: From the mid -- from mid-1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in that time, you have had a connection of working with him in separate areas of responsibility, in relation to, in his case, the government of Croatia, and, in your case, being mayor of the city of Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: In mid-1990, I was the mayor and Mr. Cermak was still a private person at the time, so he became a member of the government later on, as an assistant minister, around 1991, in mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about your observation of Mr. Cermak's organisational skills, what his qualities are. As you were able to observe them from your connections with him described in your statement, how would you describe Mr. Cermak's organisational skills?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, in mid-1990, of course, my main focus was to organise the life of the big city under new circumstances. However, parallel with that, I was the president of the Croatian football council; it was a new institution which was important and which was also opening up to Europe and its partners. And I had a chance to meet Mr. Cermak in this period as someone who was also very much committed to a social life, sports life; and we discussed a number of topics which were related both to the city and also to the sports milieu.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, this has to be translated --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to us, and --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I will do my best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please slow down --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- because I ask tell that the pace is very hot.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. So please slow down and remember the focus of my question was on Mr. Cermak's organisational skills. The Court has the information within your statement already, and what I want you to do is focus on how you perceived the quality of his organisational skills. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talked about his sports and social activities in that time, during the interregnum, Mr. Cermak was present in that milieu. And that's where his organisational abilities -- let us not forget that this was the period after the first democratic elections in the Republic of Croatia in which Mr. Cermak participated on the side of the Croatian democratic union. And his organisational abilities were expressed in the organisation of a number of public rallies and everything else that is part of the infrastructure and logistics which are very important for someone to be successful in that sort of public appearance. Later on, that is to say, in the latter half of 1991, when the war was spreading on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, when General Cermak was not yet general at the time, took part in the defence. We could talk about the continuation of his presence and of his abilities, which I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was whilst he was assistant minister for defence and involved in logistics that I want to focus on -- on now, as to the quality of the work that he was doing there, so far as you could see --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- whether he accomplished his work well or not.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Zagreb was the defence base, defence from aggression. And during the whole period, a number of people would come from across Croatia with a plea that Zagreb should help them or that they should receive help from the Ministry of Defence. And very often I would send these people from various parts of Croatia where war was going on, I would address them to Mr. Cermak who was Assistant Minister in the Ministry of Defence to help them, and each time, after a day or two, I would get the information that they communicated in a very efficient way and that he helped them. As for the city of Zagreb itself, it was not once that I asked him for advice or suggestions in view of logistics and assessment, which is often necessary in a big city, such as this one, and he always intervened in good time and in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The phrase we got was "it was not once." By that do you mean on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Much more than once. And let us not forget that war was spreading in Croatia at that time from Dalmatia to the Eastern Slavonia and every single day representatives of various municipalities came to see us in the city of Zagreb and ask us for assistance. Let us also not forget that the city of Zagreb, which has population of a million people, has population from all parts of Croatia who were willing to go out to the front and take part in the defence of various parts of Croatia. As the city of Zagreb, we could help them with typical logistics. We could provide food and clothing. However, as for the assistance that had to do with war operations that had to be done through the Ministry of Defence - and very often my personal recommendation or of someone -- of colleagues from the Executive Council was to go and see General Cermak, because of his efficiency, because the war operations could not be postponed. Sometimes it was the question not of a day but of the hour when assistance would be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Later, Mr. Cermak transferred to become the minister of the economy in -- in 1993. And in relation to that role of his, did you continue working with him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, to put it colloquially, one could say that General Cermak, as the minister of economics at the time, tried to act as a bulldozer whenever one could react to provide infrastructure that was destroyed because of the war. Whenever someone could do something to make the public utilities and communal services begin to operate in terms of restoring the economics, companies, one could note his wish and his presence and his organisational skills. If there were two complementary addresses, then certainly that was the Chamber of Commerce and the Ministry of Economics. So the nature of our work made us communicate practically every day and also cooperate on a daily base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned there "infrastructure." The importance to Croatia at this time in 1993, in repairing infrastructure damaged by war, how significant was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, that was the decisive issue. Because, without infrastructure, you cannot organise the normal life of people, let's alone the economic activities. Let us not forget that throughout this period Croatia managed to keep up manufacture and export and also a high level of employment. So even under wartime conditions and aggression, you had to go on living and have enough strength for the time that was coming which meant opening up towards the world and Europe because simply, regardless of the fact that war was being waged in Croatia, normal life just had to go on. And perhaps as a footnote, very often previously, as the mayor during the day and during the night, we also had to take into account security; and then, during the day, the services would have to issue permits and resolve daily issues of the citizens. And it was the same in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Eventually, Mr. Cermak left his post as minister of the economy to concentrate on private business. What contact and connection did you have with him from that period in October 1993 onwards to 1995 when he left the government?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Primarily we had connections as friends and personal ones. So when you go through a period of life that is so dramatic on the whole, then relations become permanent. I understood his reasons - and I mentioned them in my statement that he wanted to do more and further - but under these circumstances, the political resolutions were still dominant and that was what determined the tempo of possible activities in the country. So he had enthusiasm. He wanted to do things faster, but that was conditioned by circumstances that were beyond our possibility to have -- to effect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period from October 1993 to August 1995, was Mr. Cermak involved in any political way in -- in politics or government?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't. He turned to the area where he thought he had to be recognised, and to do his best, and that was private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In -- going back to private business, were individual steps, such as that, important for Croatia and its economy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, it was certainly so. Namely, the reconstruction of economic life in Croatia - let us not forget that the gross national product had dropped by more than one third which had happened during the big economic crisis on the international scene. So it was important. We had the opening up towards the world and that was the imperative in Croatia, because the aggression and war have its beginning and -- have their beginning and their end. But as for normal life, if it is to go on, economy has to go on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So as president of Chamber of Commerce during this period, were you supportive of the initiatives by people such as Mr. Cermak who were setting up private businesses?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Our task was much broader. We tried to connect a number of companies in Croatia and create something that is, today, called "clusters" in the contemporary colloquialism, then also to support export, to try to attract foreign investments, and also, in all parts of Croatia, support this whenever life was going back to normal. So that the Croatian Chamber of Commerce was more than a development agency, which incited, entrepreneurship and also employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to turn now to August of 1995, and to the 5th of August, the date of the conclusion of Operation Oluja and the liberation of the territories previously occupied at that time. Where were you on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I was outside Zagreb, on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And your first information about Mr. Cermak being appointed to the position of commander of the Knin Garrison came from where?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I heard it over the radio. I was listening the news and in the course of those days, radio and TV programme was omni-present in our lives, and I heard that announcement being made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you speak to Mr. Cermak about this appointment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He called me over the phone. He said that he had accepted to help, that he was urgently leaving, and he also added that he wanted me to learn of that from him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the reason for him phoning you was -- was why?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Firstly, given our friendship, it was quite normal for me to hear it from him. Secondly, he probably wanted to share his enthusiasm with me, and I could clearly feel it over the phone. He said that, I will try to continue working on what I had worked before in the Ministry of Economic Affairs and try to do something of use, perhaps in another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did give him -- or, first of all, how did he describe the work he was going to do in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, if we are to narrow that to one or two sentence, it was to create a normal living conditions asap and to create conditions for the local economy, for the people residing there, to become functioning again, to come up with a way to normalize the situation as soon as possible so that those people could feel that they were put to some good use and that they were actually useful to the community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you give him any advice?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what advice was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I told him that the establishment of utilities and a communal life and services is not as attractive as some other engagements, but it requires team-work, resources, and round the clock work and commitment. I told him that as a former president of the Executive Council and the mayor of a large city. Basically, the needs of such disparate cities are similar, be it the one million inhabitant city that is Zagreb or the town that is Knin, which had between 10 and 50.000. My first problem as a mayor was to unblock a waste dump, and that came about in the summer months. That simply was the first thing that crossed my mind when giving him the advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Upon liberation of the area, were you aware what structures for authority and responsibility were in place for Knin at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I knew that there was a governmental commissioner. I knew there were certain institutions, which I should have shouldered their part of the burden. But my knowledge was of that general level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on now to later on, after Mr. Cermak left for Knin, did you meet him after he had gone down to take up his position?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes. In the second half of August, when I returned from my leave, Mr. Cermak came to Zagreb at that time. And we met, of course, at that time and spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: In the -- in my and his office, basically, because we shared office in the same building at Martica Street, number 65, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you know the reason for Mr. Cermak coming back to Zagreb at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, if I am to summarize that, there were two important elements. Firstly, given the organisational aspect of his work, he came to speak to some people in certain governmental departments. Secondly, in relation to his business activities that was under way, to see what needed to be done by him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if, before he had gone down or before he had been appointed on the 5th of August by President Tudjman, whether there had been any previous planning in relation to him having any role in the future in Knin, whether this had been a planned appointment of him or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, and as far to the information that was available, this was supposed to be a limited activity. It was expected of him to be a link as a person who was supposed to stimulate the civilian sector and, after that, to go back home. From our conversations and what I also believe was that one person can initiate processes but cannot stand in for the entire civilian authority structure, because this needs to be shouldered by different institutions, different governmental departments, or county offices present in the area itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what governmental departments he had come up to see or whom he met on his return to Zagreb on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that specifically. In the overall pace of events, it was not particularly important to discuss the first, the second, or the fifth meeting; but two topics prevailed, in general. One, were public utilities. And his wish was to have Zagreb and other cities help Knin, primarily in terms much equipment that was missing. And from Zagreb, he also expected in some near future to assist with certain aspects of those public utilities. Regarding the economy, his wish and ambition was to have some of the companies which can manufacture parts of its production in Knin to open up their branches and plants there, thus, obtaining possible -- giving possibility for employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you give any assistance or support to him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Firstly, I expressed my understanding. As I said, I understand what public utilities mean, and I know what public -- private entrepreneurship means. But, in principle, I advised him to slow down. I told him it wasn't possible in a short period of time to do everything. I also told him to be realistic and that after liberation of a large part of Croatia, no matter the problems were that he was facing that stood in opposition to his enthusiasm, that it was necessary for the government and other cities in Croatia to help in a number of different areas. And that he had to be realistic in the sense of the scope of aid he was to receive and the period of time within which that assistance was to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if he was successful in getting any aid or assistance from other institutions outside Knin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, one can always look at things generally all in -- detail or specifically. In general terms, the needs were far greater. But specifically, given his communication ability and the respect he enjoyed as well as his links with different public figures at the time, I am positive that, under the circumstances, he achieved the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you provide the Court with any specific examples of equipment or otherwise that he was able to obtain?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: From Zagreb and Split, as two major cities in Croatia, there must be certain documents in existence about trucks and equipment he received for public utilities. But other than that, I didn't -- I do not have any knowledge of particular details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the few months, say, three or four months after his appointment to Knin, on how many occasions did you meet him? Was it just that one occasion, or were there other occasions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Looking back, I think it was on one or two other occasions, because frequently he had no time to visit Zagreb. In those few occasions, I noticed that he became more aware of the restrictions of his communication with the commissioner. And he was slowly realizing that as an individual, he was less and less indispensable. And that it was up to those who represented the institutions to take over their responsibilities step by step, and primarily I have in mind the different governmental departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all the questions I ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Any cross-examination by counsel for Mr. Gotovina or Mr. Cermak -- Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Vedris?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vedris.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to start, first, with clarifying some of the function -- the functions had you in the 1990s. We heard this morning, and it's part of your statement, that you were the first in the 1990s, in effect the mayor of Zagreb, and then also president of the Crisis Staff of the city of Zagreb. And then, from April 1992 onwards, you were the minister without portfolio in the Croatian government. Until when you did have that function?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was up until late October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then on the 29th of December, 1992, until 4th of March, 1993, you were, as we hard, the Deputy Prime Minister for economy. Did you resign --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Deputy Prime Minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [In English] okay, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you resign with immediate effect on 4th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you continued to attend meetings at the presidential palace with President Tudjman and other participants and the president still addressed you with Deputy Prime Minister. And I'm talking about the meeting on 12th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: That is possible, because, at the time, I still acted as a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. We heard you talking about the organisational capabilities of Mr. Cermak, and you talk extensively about that in your witness statement. On various occasions, you address his exceptional organisational skills. I want to ask you, did you know that Mr. Cermak had probably in the -- in 1990, perhaps even earlier or slightly later, his own unit of 800 men, armed men, at the time before the Croatian army existed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to address that because I don't know what the background do this question is, and -- in terms of establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, whatever the background of the question is, could you please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is totally unclear to me how it could be -- the background of the question could be relevant before you answered that, Mr. Vedris. That comes as a bit of a surprise. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's have a look at a document and see whether it refreshes, perhaps, your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is P2355, an interview Mr. Cermak gave in 1997 to Nacional, and I'm interested in the English, page 3, and in B/C/S, in Croatian, it's on page 2. Yes, this is in B/C/S, and in B/C/S, the question put to him starts in the third column from the right to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You see it in bold "veliki minusi u MORH." There the question starts. And in English, it's on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have an English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you now have it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just come on, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at one time we should move the B/C/S so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] Sorry, on the left side is the Croatian with a huge, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right, English. May I ask you to concentrate on Croatian side, and can you give me exact paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we will focus on B/C/S for a moment, with Mr. Kay's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if we focus on the right bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Can you put in bigger form?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it will come up very soon. And we need to go to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There you see "veliki minusi u MORH" in bold, and that's the question that I'm interested in, Nacional.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm. And was the point in this question in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't not finish, so we need to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, just give Mr. Waespi some time to organise what he wants to show you on the screen. And I noticed that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- highly gave up of efficiency --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and good organisation. Mr. Waespi is doing his utmost best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Mr. Vedris. Let's move to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And now it's the second column to the right from the top, and you see the continuance of the answer of Mr. Cermak. And in about the tenth line you see the reference to the 800 armed men.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just ask the Registrar to put on the English version, bottom of page 3, and then it's continuing on page 4, but I'm only interested in what is at the bottom of the page 3. And I can read it out, what General Cermak responded to a question: "After it became obvious that the war would not be avoided, I started preparing my own unit before the ZNG and the Croatian army were established. By then, I had over 800 armed men. At the beginning, I have my HQ at the Radicev Trg, where I was the presidential advisor on special affairs." Now, does that refresh your memory about these 800 men? Perhaps you don't know, but perhaps it refreshes your memory.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: This is the background, and now it all becomes clear. In Croatia, there were legal security companies. They were fully legal. And each of their members, who had a weapon on him, had a licence too. By sheer circumstance, I'm more familiar with it through my function as the president of the Croatian soccer association because soccer games at that time were high-risk events. And in addition to regular police escort provided to both supporters and the teams, security companies participated as well. While now we are on the topic of refreshing our memories, I can tell you there were several such security companies which working within the legal framework, pursuing their business activities and purchasing weapons legally, I reiterate. As regards the other part of Mr. Cermak's answer, but given -- that is something I don't know. But what I can tell you was that he participated actively in the first multi-party elections as part of the HDZ, and I presume that was a part of that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, if you know, Mr. Cermak would pay these 800 mean and he would give them tasks? Is that the way it went?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: No. The regular security companies had their own regular tasks. They were engaged on securing specific facilities, institutions, banks, the public sector, and that was how they earned their wages, and that's where the wages for the employees came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who gave the tasks to these 800 armed men?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: The one who was giving them tasks was the person who was heading the company, depending on the contracts that the company. They had a schedule of daily duties, and they organised it in the same way that the work of security companies is organised to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the boss of these 800 armed men was General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm a bit concerned about your line of questioning. The witness tells us that the 800 men were - as I understand it - that they were employed by a firm which was headed by Mr. Cermak. And as in -- as we find often in these kind of firms, that they were sent to someone who had hired security. And your questions seem to ignore, more or less, that you have always two levels. The one is those who are in charge of the company who make the contract and say, Well, you need 20 security mean. Here, you've got a list. When do you want them to be there? 9.00 in the morning. What is their task? To secure a building or to secure a person or ... And then the other level is that the one who has hired such security, that he says, We'll go do Zagreb this morning, or you should -- better look at the back of the building than the front of the building because that's where we expect the risk to be greater or that's where construction works are done and that there's a special risk. So if we're talking about boss -- about tasks, et cetera, could you, in view of the answer of the witness, please clearly keep in mind which of the two levels we are focussing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. President. I'm interested in the ultimate ownership, if you want, of these 800 mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was the -- in general, at the high strategic level, not at a daily level, who was the chief, if you want, of these 800 mean. That was Mr. Cermak. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I think that this is confusion. There was no strategic boss. These were companies that were recorded in the court register, they had their management, their owners, and they also had their business contracts that were concluded mostly with the banking sector and public institutions, and they were doing their job. Everything else is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, let me go back --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: It's an issue of possible co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let me go back to what Mr. Cermak said in his interview. I quote: "By then, I had over 800 men, and I had my HQ at this Radicev Trg." So what was the role of General Cermak in relation to these 800 men, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But if you allow me a brief comment. Namely, at the time, in Croatia and in Zagreb, we were also the target of many possible provocations; I primarily mean the sports events. All the sports events that had an international character were potential powder kegs, and it was precisely the security companies that, alongside their regular weekly duties, we would engage them at the sports events in order to avoid possible conflict or provocations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that the buses with the fans would leave in an orderly way and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly had to be done at football events is not the focus of Mr. Waespi, his question. Let me try to see whether I have understood well what he'd like to hear from -- to know from you. Who was the owner of the firm that employed the security people that you could hire from that company? Who opened that firm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the court registers exist, and it is very easy to establish who are also the owners and the management of the company. I have no direct knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, if you don't know -- okay. You say it is registered, but you do not know. Second question --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, that is so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you don't know who owns the firm, you don't know who managed the firm. Now, if you made a contract from your football position, if you would hire security, with whom would you speak and negotiate about the contract?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The procedure was as follows: The Croatian soccer association as the institution and their chief secretary or specific clubs would then simply communicate by phone or in any other way with a specific security company, because, of course, there was a number of them, they would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's try to immediately focus on what seems to be the core of the issue. Did the football association ever hire security from a firm, a security firm in which Mr. Cermak was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no direct knowledge about this, because the chief secretary and the administration were in charge of this, and not myself as the president. But, of course, all the relevant documents are still in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say: I do not know "because the ... secretary and the administration were in charge of this, and not myself as the president." Sometimes presidents do know what their staff are doing. Simple question: Are you aware of any security contract concluded between the football association and a firm, in which Mr. Cermak, either as owner, manager, or whatever way, played a role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, considering the levels of responsibility, considering the segments of work that people were in charge of, considering my position and positions, I was fully concentrated on providing as much security for public law and order as possible. And I cannot answer this, because I wasn't involved in this procedurally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you not whether it was important to get security. I did not ask you whether your position required you to get involved. I just asked you whether you know whether the football association ever hired security from a firm in which Mr. Cermak was involved. Did they; or did they not; or don't you know? If you say, I do not know, you do not have to explain why, because the explanations usually -- well, let's refrain from and comment on explanations. Do you know that this ever happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there was a number of companies on the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, was one of these companies -- was there one company in which Mr. Markac -- Mr. Cermak was involved in any way, to your knowledge? Ownership, management, other consulting capacity? Was there any firm of which you know that Mr. Cermak was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I know, he had business and friendly relations with some of these companies and their owners, but I don't know of any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever a -- could you tell us with which of these companies he had such friendly relationships with what may have been the owners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, looking back, I remember one name. I think it was the company named Sokol Safranic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was there ever a contract concluded between the football association and this company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, so any answer that I would give would not be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vedris, you talk a lot about President Tudjman in your witness statement. I think you mentioned him at least ten times. You talk about his motives and plans. Paragraph 12 in relations to the appointments of Cermak; his desires, paragraph 4. How well did you know Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Well, considering how dramatic the events were in the period when I held public positions, I quite often had a chance to communicate with President Tudjman. And, of course, I came to know a few things about his political and public activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also attended quite a few meetings under his -- his chairmanship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that even continues as we heard earlier today, after you stopped being a Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr. Waespi could be more specific as to which portions of the paragraphs he is challenging. I don't see that he is -- the statement refers to Mr. Tudjman's motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not challenging anything. I'm just saying that the witness talked in his witness statements, in paragraph 12, about his motives and plans in relation to the appointment of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's just -- I noticed some exhibits on the exhibit list. So if it goes outside the scope, I would like to put an objection. But if that's the case, if it's just related to Mr. Cermak, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said this -- that he has mentioned at least ten times. And examples are the paragraphs I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, here's my objection. If the Prosecution intends to challenge any motives that President Tudjman had vis-a-vis Mr. Cermak, which is what I have been told is -- he is referring to in the statement, I have no objection. If the Prosecution intends to explore President Tudjman's views generally about issues that are not specifically discussed in the statement, then I would say that it's outside the scope of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's hear what questions Mr. Waespi will further put to the witness, and we, and also Mr. Waespi, has in the back of his mind, what would be your objection if we would enter a certain area. Apart from cross-examination not being limited to what was dealt with in chief -- our rules there's no strict rule to say you can only deal with matters which were touched upon in chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I was about to put to you that you even attended meetings with President Tudjman when you were the president of the Chamber of commerce; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at these meetings, a whole range of topics was discussed, from economy, from issues in Bosnia, and whatever was on the agenda of these topics, of these meetings you attended.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Of course. When I was there and when concern topics were discussed, I think that the written minutes also exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me talk about President Tudjman's style of government or leadership. Now, I think it was your own view that the H - and I quote: "The HDZ and Croatia have become Bolshevik manner totalitarian organisation." Is that a quote that can be attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Would be so kind to provide the entire document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But let me ask you first: Do you remember having made a comment in this regard, talking about Bolshevik manner totalitarian organisation. I will show you a document in a moment, but I'm interested in whether you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I wish to see the original document probably in Croatian, then we would see the character of the translation, and then I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first answer the question. And then if there is any need we will look at whatever document there is. And if the translation has to be checked, we will carefully do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We might talk about the level of authoritarianism, I think that would be the right expression, and this is why I asked to see the document in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply, Mr. Vedris, was whether you remember having made a comment in talking about Bolshevik manner, totalitarian organisation. Do you recollect -- have any recollection of having given such a comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, without seeing the document and the background, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can answer the question in whether you have any recollection having made such a statement. If there's any need to look at a document, with may do so, or we may refrain from doing that. But you're here, first of all, to answer the question, which is not a question about what we find in a document, but which is a question about your recollection of making a certain statement. If you know, tell us; if you have no recollection, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember without having insight into the wider background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vedris, this is not an answer to the question. This is a conditional answer. If you have recollection, please, tell us; if you don't remember, tell us, I don't remember. But don't try to make this answer a conditional one. So to say: I do not remember unless the sun shines tomorrow. That's not the kind of answer we're expecting. If you have a recollection of having said such -- of given such a comment, tell us. If you say, My recollection, I have never made such a statement; that's another possible answer. Or it may be or it may not be, but I don't remember at this moment. Give us the answer but not conditions or I have to look at the document first. We do not even know whether there's a document. Please proceed, with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that I did say so, but I would wish to see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so your answer is it is possible but you do not know four sure. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we do understand that you would wish to see a document in which we find any reflection of you having made such a statement. I leave it in the hands of Mr. Waespi, whether or not he will put this document to you now. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I would like to go to 65 ter 7459.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Vedris, is a meeting dated 3rd March, 1995, between President Tudjman and at least Mr. Ivica Crnic. And I would like you to have a look at the cover page first. And we don't need to go into any detail, except for the passage I'm interested in. But the transcript shows a conversation between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Crnic. And President Tudjman appears to be fairly angry with Mr. Crnic. Now, tell me first, who is Mr. Crnic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crnic is a respectable lawyer from Croatia, from Zagreb, who held a number of public positions, and is he now a lawyer at Radio Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we go in English page 3 and B/C/S page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We see that President Tudjman accuses Mr. Crnic of destabilising Croatia with his conduct. So that's basically what this much of the conversation is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And let's go to page 10 in English. And in Croatian, it's page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I read out the part I'm interested in. Actually in English it starts at page 9. "President Tudjman: You see, Croatian people will not let that happen in spite of those acts, no matter if you or anybody else participate in that. "Ivica Crnic: Any way, I do not participate in any organisation or any clan. I swore in health of my daughter, and the man does not swear just like this in those things. "President: It is surprising. As far as I know, even though you say you're not in any clan with Nikica, Mladen was your friend. Mladen Verdis actually wrote the same pamphlet that HDZ and this Croatia have become Bolshevik manner totalitarian organization. "Yes that is what you are giving us, isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The whole question was prefaced by Mr. Vedris having said something about being Bolshevistic. Now, what we hear is that it was something that might have been written and he is not being confronted that he himself said or I himself wrote, but he is being confronted with a transcript that gives basically a third-hand account of what possibly might have been said. And I think that is very unfair, given all of the prefacing that we had to this questioning with the transcript to be used in this manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, what this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- transcript reveals is that a quote, a very straightforward quote, easily recognisable quote, was attributed to Mr. Vedris. Whether he said it or wrote it doesn't matter. And I asked him beforehand whether he remembers having made the quote and he said, It's possible; I'd like to see the document. So I see no objectionable way that I can put the transcript to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a document; it's not the article. It's a transcript which is basically a third-hand reference. I think it's extremely unfair to this witness to present it in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was asked whether he ever gave a comment; that was the language which was used in at least most of the questions. The witness was reluctant to answer a question from his memory. It took me quite a while to get him there. And then he said -- no, Mr. Vedris, I'm speaking at this moment. Then I urged him to answer the question, and he asked to see a document, where Mr. Waespi now puts the document on the table. And we all can see what the document contains. That is, a comment by the president in which he refers to what others have said or -- not have said but what Mr. Vedris wrote. Mr. Waespi may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you ever utter these word, write them down in a pamphlet, or make any other comment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Your Honours and Mr. Prosecutor, if I did, in the course of such a conversation, I must have surely told the president that Croatia must be wary of continuing its path --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not answer the question of Mr. Waespi. If I did it, then ... Mr. Waespi just asked you a rather simple question, and you're invited to answer the question. Did you ever utter these words, write them down in a pamphlet, or make any other comment, which I understand to be whether you ever, in any other context, uttered such terms. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I never wrote that in any pamphlets. Whether I said anything of the sort in a discussion, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know what the president is referring to, what kind of pamphlet?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at the clock. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will move on from the document, which I'd like to make an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll object to the admission under Rule 89(C). I don't see any relevance or probative value in this document. And without having had an opportunity to read what else is in the document, I would object if this is the sole basis for tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, is there any other part of this document or would you just focus on the observation made by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact it's on the back part. There's another comment towards the end of the document. But I'm only interested in -- in the comment actually read out. But I think it is important to have the document in. Also, because of the fact that the witness wanted to see the document. The witness is mentioned. He had the chance to comment on it. I think there is sufficient foundation laid to have it tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness wanted to see a document where he himself said that, not a document where there was something third hand. And I disagree with the assertion that the entire portion of this -- or this entire transcript, even this particular portion, is relevant or probative for any issue relating to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objections are denied. But the Chamber will admit only the portion specifically dealt with. That is, cover page and relevant page, where the president makes his statement. Perhaps the page prior to that; I leave it up to the parties to see whether that's needed for the context. Because I noticed that in English the -- what the president says is rather at the top of the page which might make it a bit more difficult to have the clear view on the context. So, therefore, Mr. Waespi, you are invited to tender the relevant portion of this document and to consider during the next break whether you can agree with the Defence teams in what would be appropriate context, half a page, whole page, and whether the page shown to us, as such, gives sufficient context as far as what follows. We'll hear from you after the break. We'll first have a break. And we will resume at 11.00. Mr. Waespi, by the way, could you give us any impression, as far as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll certainly conclude within the next session. I think maybe another -- less than an hour, I would assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If possible, I do not know whether -- we have two witnesses scheduled for today, if all parties could do their utmost best to see whether we can conclude the testimony of both witnesses today, that would be appreciated. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially in view of the Chamber urging the parties to see whether we could finish today, the Chamber apologises for the late start which was caused by urgent Tribunal matters. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In relation to the last proposed exhibit, 65 ter 7459, we suggest that pages 9 and 10 in English and 14 to 16 in Croatian be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has decided on admission, is there any comment on the contextualisation of the relevant portion? If not ... Then, Mr. Registrar the -- And the cover page as well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, may I take it that this portion has been uploaded or will be uploaded into e-court so that you verify, together with the Registrar, whether we have the right portion of the document in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vedris, leaving aside the Bolshevik characterisation, how would you describe Mr. Tudjman's style of leadership?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: As a very young democracy springing up in very difficult conditions of war, where a border-line between procedure and wishes for efficiency is rather difficult to arrive at. This is basically how I describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your answer. But let me maybe put it in a different way. Stipe Mesic publicly called him a dictator. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to the form of the question. I'm not sure what Stipe Mesic has to do with anything. And if he wants to ask the witness's opinion about something that's fine, but then to put to him what some other person may have said, I don't see the probative value in that, and I think it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Waespi, let's me just check that. Well, Mr. Waespi started asking about how the witness viewed the -- the style of leadership. And then, as such, to put to a witness the assessment of that -- others, that is not, I would say, in cross-examination, is not inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I suspect may happen is that this is sort of bootstrapping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well let me just state, because I'm going to object to the admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but one thing, Mr. Misetic. The witness understands English. I just wanted to remind you that whatever comments you make at this moment should not be of a kind to inappropriately come to the knowledge of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going talk about substance of testimony. What I will say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would will describe what kind of a trap you expect to be there, that, of course, could, under circumstances, be a message to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting there is a trap. What I'm saying is that it's bootstrapping, because now the question has been posed about what the third person thinks. Then to show him documents about what the third person thinks, we will object, and then the argument coming back will be, Well the witness was asked questions about it, he commented about it; therefore it has probative value. Therefore, let's get it in. My objection is the same objection that was litigated previously in this case with respect to P687, at transcript page 6851, which is putting materials to a witness about what someone else commented, that otherwise have no relationship, to the witness is improper. It denies us the right to cross-examine the witness who is not in court. And if that is the exercise that we're going to go through, then I wish to put it now on the record that we're going to object to a procedure and an argument later that says, Well, I asked him all sorts of questions about Mr. Mesic, and, therefore, to make the transcript clean, we need to admit these other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your position, Mr. Misetic. I think that if Mr. Waespi would share with you that Mr. -- whoever, Mr. X, Y, or Z, has said something. And if he puts that to the witness that if you do not disagree that this person has once said that, that there is no need to have that document be admitted into evidence, would there? Because then it's just the quote and nothing else. And then the mere fact that X, Y, or Z would have said A, B, or C just to put to the witness, there would be no further probative value in such a document, and therefore, there would be no need to have it admitted into -- into evidence, unless you would challenge that Mr. A, B, or C would have ever been reported to have said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And I agree with you, Your Honour, that the provisio that that wouldn't mean that we agree that that becomes the substance of evidence because it was within -- embedded in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's -- I think that's clear, that whoever is quoted, you have had no opportunity to cross-examine that person about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, for our the part, we agree with the approach of Mr. Misetic there, because we would challenge the validity of undergoing a form of cross-examination in that way. It has no probative value at all to -- to say, Well, this person says this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether he was right or wrong in that quote is, of course, Mr. Waespi, I take it, is not something that you would conclude on the basis of putting a quote to this witness, would it? It's just to perhaps to test the answer the witness has given?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's about starting with a credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Testing this witness, and not seeking the substance of the quote to -- to create evidence. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What I want from the witness is his assessment of the style of leadership in 1992, 1993, 1995. He was a minister at that time; I want a realistic, fair assessment of how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic. Yes, Mr. Kay, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, just for the record, I do want to join in my [sic] objection. And if that's what's being asked of the witness, what his view or opinion is, I don't have a problem with that. But to confront him with what someone else thinks or believes is really not relevant or probative. So I just wanted to join in those objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's hardly appropriate in cross-examination to put whatever we have of which, I think, have good-faith belief in to put it to the witness. That's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just as a result of the exchange there, one with can see what else lies in -- in relation to this matter. If it's to test a witness's credibility, you're bound by his answer. And that is a very accepted rule, because you are putting something to him which is outside the evidence of -- of the case. And it can't that be you rely on because someone else said this and you've put it to him, and the witness then denies it, that you have somehow challenged his credibility. The actual rule is this: You are bound by that answer. You're not actually challenging the witness's credibility. You are bound by the answer of it. And that is a very accepted rule in all common law jurisdictions in relation to this process, because -- for obvious reason, none of us are able to deal with it. But the answer that Mr. Waespi gets, whatever it is, on whatever matter which is extraneous to the materials in the Court, he is bound by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer given by this witness on the matter. At the same time, we should not forget that -- and that's, of course, to some extent triggered by the statement itself and is not uncommon in the courtrooms in this house, that is, that we're not only talking about facts, but we are talking about impressions, opinions, et cetera. And this is part of it. And, therefore, Mr. Waespi, as I said before, the Chamber will not -- will allow you to put these questions. But let's also not forget that what witness A, B, or C, or a person quoted in the press thinks about the quality of -- or the colour of the eyes of another person is, of course -- is not always directly addressing the core of the case. So, therefore, you would -- we would certainly not encourage you to put all the qualifications of the style of leadership of Mr. Tudjman to this witness and then to find out that he disagrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mesic, he is a friend of yours, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let me ask you the question again. Mr. Mesic publicly called Mr. Tudjman a dictator; in fact, even in relation to how the lineup of the football team should be done. And you were, as you testified this Monday, president of the football association. Now, do you agree with Mr. Mesic that Mr. Tudjman was a dictator?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: No. I think he was prone to authoritarianism to some extent, but he had respect for parliamentary democracy and it's institutions. While we're on the subject of soccer, I can tell you that he never tried to impose anything on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go then to a different 65 ter. This is 7463. This is a speech by Mr. Mesic taken from his official home page, November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, here we are reaching, of course, the issue, if you want to use another qualification used by Mr. Mesic. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, it goes to what the witness said, the answer about the football team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the football team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least we are back in the field of facts. Football is fact. I do understand that, at least, in the country of which the -- this Tribunal is established, that we have 16 million coaches of the Dutch national team. That is at least how it is described, the situation. If we are now back in the realm of facts, could you please tell us what you want, what your quote will be or what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's a couple of sentences. He talks not only, of course, about the football team but also what the witness just says, that Mr. Tudjman had respect for parliament. That is not what Mr. Mesic, the successor of Mr. Tudjman, says. I would like to put this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Misetic. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I would like that the witness, who gives a one-sided view of the way it was at the time, he uses the word democracy, and I want the Trial Chamber and the witness to know that there this is an different view from a very very respected person. And I want the witness to -- to give an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, he had his case in chief; he didn't call Mesic. He didn't call a single witness to discuss Mr. Tudjman's style of governing. Now he has opened a line of examination that the witness didn't discuss in direct examination, doesn't like the answer, and now wishes to impeach the witness with the statement of someone who is not in court. And he didn't make a discussion in his direct examination about democratic style or not. That's an answer to a topic that he's opened in cross-examination. And to my earlier objection, Mr. President, you indicated that he can go outside the scope of direct. He's now outside the scope of direct, trying to impeach a witness for an answer that wasn't raised in direct examination. And now we're into the area that exactly I had objected to earlier, which is, he wants to get testimony in of another witness who he failed to call in his case in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to reiterate what I said before. I'd like this witness who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, you are -- the objection came from the Defence, so you're now -- the last one -- after I give an opportunity to the other Defence counsel to either join or add something to what Mr. Misetic said, then have you an opportunity to respond, Mr. Waespi, and then the Chamber will rule on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were asked for a focused case. And one wonders, with this approach, as to who is giving evidence here. Stipe Mesic or Mladen Verdis; whose evidence is under consideration? It must be Mr. Vedris's evidence that is under consideration, what he says and what he knows, not what other people have said and may believe they know, because we don't know the basis for any other external statement. In my submission, this is not the focused case Your Honour requested and said to the Defence at the start of the Defence cases when we go down these routes. Questions to Mr. Vedris as to his knowledge, his information, what he knows, provides that focus. To now embark from a small question about Mr. Mesic to materials that Mr. Mesic may have produced, who knows? He may have rejected what he said. He may have said that he uttered views for political gain for himself. There can be all manner of reasons, and what we move from is this witness to someone else's statements. That, in my submission, cannot be the proper basis for cross-examination. It's not something the Defence did, and in my submission, it's not something the Prosecution should be allowed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to add our joinder to both of the objections and just add one other thing. It's obvious that if Mr. Vedris had written or said in the past that Mr. Tudjman was a dictator, it would be completely relevant to bring something like this up for him. We're getting further and further afield and further and further deluded from the issue. The issue is of Mr. Vedris's credibility not -- not Mr. Tudjman's or Mr. Mesic's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, first of all, to the point Mr. Kay made. This is not something Stipe Mesic said in passing. As I said before, this is from a speech, official speech Mr. Mesic gave. It's available on the home page. Second, we have witnesses, I think Mr. Galbraith talked about Mr. Tudjman and his style of government, this is part of our case. And I believe the Prosecution, with every Defence witness, we are entitled to elicit evidence that's favourable to us.
