Now, the witness said a moment ago that Mr. Tudjman had respect for the parliament. So I believe I'm entitled to put to the witness information that's contradictory of this point. So Your Honours can check the credibility of this witness on that point. This is an very short portion, I think about eight lines, and the witness can say whether he would disagree or whether he would accept what Mr. Mesic said on this point. This is basic cross-examination, in my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the Chamber allows you to -- to briefly put this quote as the last one for the time being, unless, of course, we never know whether, from the answer of the witness, something very special arises. But then to formulate your question. And then before you answer that question, Mr. Vedris, the Chamber will first consider whether the question is one that needs to be answered by you. So we'll give the green light in answering, or red light, for the answer of the question. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to 65 ter 7463. And in English, it's on top of page 5; and in B/C/S it's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me read what President Mesic said in November 2000: "Although the system in force is usually designated as a semi-presidential, it was actually a presidential one. And even more than that, Franjo Tudjman took all the decisions on the appearance of the state seal, on the appointment of special ministers, but also on the selector of the Croatian football team. At the same time, Croatia was a strictly centralised country with the centre making all the decisions and everybody leaving for the centre. The government reported to the president and not to the parliament." Now, you talked a moment ago about the issue of -- of the parliament vis-a-vis President Tudjman and also, and this is obviously a minor issue, about the Croatian football team. Now, having read what Mr. Mesic stated, do you agree with him, or do you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not possible to answer with a yes or a no because we are talking about different periods of time. I can talk about the period when I was actively involved in the public life and when I cooperated with President Tudjman. The statement we are talking about here relates to a broader period and beyond the period of my active communication with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Waespi, rather than to -- to stay with all this, if there's anything, for example, if you -- I'm not suggesting that it would be the football that is most important, but, of course, you could ask follow-up questions: Are aware of President Tudjman ever interfering with the composition of the national team? And then the witness will tell us whether he knows or not. Apart from the relevance of that, I don't expect, as a matter of fact, the Spanish king -- I wouldn't -- let me say the following. I would not know exactly what to think about if the Spanish king would ever be involved in the composition of the -- of the Spanish national team. I would not know, as a matter of fact, how that relates to matters which are at stake in the context in which the matter is raised. You could also interpret this as, That's what we want, a head of state, with such an interest in national sports. That's a different way of looking at it. So, therefore, I'm reminding you of all this so that we should not spend too much time on matters which are so multi-interpretable that it causes more confusion than anything else. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I invite Mr. Waespi to put the players that were selected, if we get into the fine detail of it, as a way of proving his knowledge and any basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- -- I join you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... question I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I join you in getting to facts rather than to opinions, assessments, et cetera. Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The question I actually have for the witness is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told, this morning, that you were part of all these meetings or many meetings you attended with Mr. Tudjman even as a president of the Chamber of Commerce. Why can you not give us your impression of the leadership style of President Tudjman at that time you were with him, 1992, 1993, 1994, until you relinquished your job as Chamber of Commerce? What prevents you from telling us whether you agree with Mr. Mesic's assessment or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, Mr. Mesic, at least from what I can see, doesn't give any time-frame. So, therefore, if this witness tells us that the leadership, style of leadership, may not have been the same during all times and that, therefore, he cannot answer the question, then it's next logical question would be: During the period when you attended meetings with President Tudjman, whether, during that period, the style of leadership substantial pages [indiscernible] substantial pages. That would be the first question. And then the follow-up questions would be about what the style of leadership was, as observed by this witness, if it did not change, and if it did change in that period of time, first, how it was in the beginning, what then changed, and how it was in the end, or whether there were more changes, to approach it an organised analytical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to move on. It will be another quote, but it's more tied to what the witness said in his witness statement. I accept the witness's answer that he doesn't want to go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 3 of your statement which is now D1772 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Waespi. But to some extent he has answered the question on page 43, line 19. He answered: "No I think he was prone to authoritarianism" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, but Mr. -- of course, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answer which, of course, is on the record now, is part of the testimony. And I think Mr. Waespi was about to move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something entirely different. That's the impression I gained. And therefore, there's no need to go back to what was earlier said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do understand that, Your Honour. My point was that he did -- Mr. Waespi said he didn't want to answer the question and he did answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to some extent he did answer the question. In certain respects he did, in others he did not. He made reservations. Let's not, at this moment, lose ourselves in -- in assessing whether the observation that he did not answer the question was without merit, was without -- Let's just move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In D1772, which is your witness statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps this document could be MFI'd, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The last one. The one I quoted from which is 65 ter 7463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it was a literal quote from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a speech of Mr. Mesic. And if there was anything relevant in there, that it is contained in the quote, and that therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that there is more. Given the objections of the Defence, I'm -- for the time being, I don't wanted to tender it, but just to have the record clear, to have it MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To have it MFI'd or to have it admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If he is not tendering it, then why MFI it, if he is not tendering it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not insisting. It's a practical issue. If the documents needs to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the document needs to be used, perhaps later we can start from zero. So if there is no objection to MFI, I'm not talking about this witness but another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nightmare for -- for a president of a Trial Chamber is to have a long MFI list, Mr. Waespi. You know that you quoted from a speech given by Mr. Stipe Mesic. Now I take it that there are no other speeches with literally the same paragraph - not eight lines, by the way, but nine lines. So, therefore, if you want to revisit this matter at any later stage, the Chamber, even without this document being MFI'd, thinks that you would find it back and then put it to any other witness that would come and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see any reason why this document should be MFIed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your witness statement, paragraph 3, and this is D1772, I quote, you say the following: "Due to permanent provocation by the political leadership in Belgrade and the JNA, a conviction started to form slowly that it was also necessary to realise and prepare for the worst and the most difficult scenario, which was armed conflict and war." But you would agree with me, Mr. Vedris, that this was not a one-sided picture, but that in particular, President Tudjman made many moves which simply had to antagonise the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: I would not agree with this. Namely, from the very beginning, from the first independent democratic elections in Croatia, it was absolutely a political and social wish to realize a democratic framework for resolving any conflict without any tendency towards antagonism, with any segment of the society.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, unfortunately, we have to go into the same issue. I would like to put a quote from Mr. Mesic which directly is in contradiction of what Mr. Metic [sic] said to this witness, and it comes from the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just trying to find the line, Mr. Waespi. But I think that we would allow you one more. I think that's what I said at the time. And you have taken that opportunity. And that should be understood as one more is not two more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is on page 4 in English of 65 ter 746 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Waespi, you must have misunderstood my ruling. Now, I'll find -- if the parties could assist me where I said "one more time," then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was already a while ago -- Judge Gwaunza tells me that it's 45:16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it is page 47, beginning at line 17 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 47. Let me be clear, Mr. Waespi, I think it was clear that the Chamber would allow to you put one more quote of Mr. Mesic to this witness that we'd then move on. And, as I said, you've taken that opportunity, and we therefore now move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's also true - is it not? - that Mr. Tudjman did not believe in a peaceful co-existence of the Croats and the Krajina Serbs. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you. President Tudjman was convinced that it was possible within Croatia to have that co-existence of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if Mr. Mesic publicly said the opposite, you would not agree with him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: You see, for agreement and for co-existence, two sides are necessary. So one cannot talk about unilateral acts of one side if you don't have the willingness of the other side, for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying one side was willing but the other side was not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, let me remind you that Croatia accepted Z-4 which envisaged a high level of independence within one and the same country, and the other side did not accept this plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we are moving far away from the statement of the witness, where I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll go back to the statement. Actually, I'm about to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You -- in your statement you say a number of times that Mr. Tudjman was impressed by Mr. Cermak and his ability and that he called him four times, I believe, to -- I think become -- for a function. Now, do you agree with me that Mr. Cermak had been one of Mr. Tudjman's favourites and that this fact was well-known?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: President Tudjman respected qualities of certain persons, and, in accordance with that, under circumstances which were not simple, these were the circumstances of war and everything else that was going on. He tried to find a position for everyone where these people could be engaged in the best way possible, with best efficiency. In the case of Mr. Cermak, I emphasised in my statement his exceptional organisational talent, which President Tudjman had seen on the occasion of the first democratic elections at the party level. This was confirmed under difficult wartime circumstances, and it was then fully expressed during the reconstruction of the country, when he worked as the minister of the economy. And these are the facts that I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So Mr. Cermak was one of the favourites of Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, whether he was a favourite or not, in the statement it's clear that this witness takes the position that President Tudjman held Mr. Cermak in high esteem for his qualities. And then to say, Are you a favourite, are you not? That really doesn't add that much. But I take it that, in view of your last question, that you want to put that someone else would have ever said Mr. Cermak was Mr. Tudjman's favourite or not, that really doesn't assist the Chamber very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any more questions, but I think there is a fine distinction between professional capabilities on one side and the word "favourite" and going beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we're done -- who assesses that and on what basis? And -- unless you say that I have a political statement in which someone explains on the basis of what facts he came to the conclusion and that Mr. Cermak was a favourite and then also explains what that means to be a favourite of -- then it would make sense. But if someone else would have said, Well all knew that Mr. Cermak was one of President Tudjman's favourites, that's -- then a personal assessment, including what others were supposed to agree with and test it. It just doesn't assist the Chamber. Unless, as I said before, you have something factual, very concrete, then to put to the witness. But just a one-liner, We all knew that four times, Mr. Cermak being one of the -- one of the babies of President Tudjman doesn't assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, I have one question for you, which is the following: Mr. Waespi put to you an interview in which Mr. Cermak was reported to have said about his 800 men. Mr. Waespi asked: Were you aware of Mr. Cermak having 800 men, armed men. And then, in response to that question, you started explaining to us what the structure of firms selling security in Croatia was and it was all legal, et cetera. You remember that? Then I did put a few questions to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did put a few questions to you about your knowledge of Mr. Cermak being engaged in whatever capacity in such a firm, and the Chamber noticed that you could not say anything about that. What the Chamber does not fully understand yet, and perhaps you could explain that to us, that if a question is put to you about Mr. Cermak having 800 men, that you start talking about the security firms and explaining in quite some detail on how that went, and then asked about Mr. Cermak's involvement in such a firm. You say, I don't know anything about it. What made you link the security firms to the 800 men of Mr. Cermak, where, in your later answers, you seemed to have no clue about Mr. Cermak being involved in such a firm, or such firms? Could you please explain that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what specifically do you think I should refer to? Whether the activity of these firms or the links that Mr. Cermak may have had with such firms? What exactly is your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is why, when asked about 800 armed men for Mr. Cermak, why do you then start talking about security firms; whereas, in your later answer, we gained the impression - and I'm saying "we" for the whole of the Chamber - that you were not aware of any link of Mr. Cermak to a security firm? How you first linked Mr. -- the 800 men to security firms; and later said, Well, Mr. Cermak and security firms; I've got no idea. To say it a bit bluntly. That is what is a puzzle for the Chamber. I wouldn't say inconsistency between the two answers, but at least --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have difficulties to understand. Please proceed with an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. In this period, you did not have two groups of 800 men. There were 800 men who were engaged as working for security firms, and I tried to explain how these firms operated and what their line of work was. So these were the armed persons. As for the interview and the quotation from it that was presented here, there is an reference to Mr. Cermak. And I said in the first part of my statement that he had business and friendly relations with some of the management an owners of such companies. And that was the context of what is mentioned in the interview. So, informally speaking, he co-operated with the firms that had the -- the firms had the employees who were armed, but they were lawfully armed, so one can talk about his cooperation, whether private or business, with the management and the owners of such companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell us who the owners were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in the first part of my testimony that there are very clear court records and there's the register from which one can see who were the owners of such companies, legally, and transparently. But it is difficult for me, after so many years, to talk about the names or the ownership structure of these companies, but documents exist and they may be presented to the Court at any given time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the suggestion that registers always transparently show real ownership is a suggestion which might not be followed by all lawyers without any hesitation. Let me be clear on that. But if you say that you knew that Mr. Cermak was doing business and had friendly relations with owners and managers, then to tell the Chamber, Go and check the registers, rather than to tell us with whom, then, Mr. Cermak had these relations or did business with, comes a bit as a surprise. Why don't you just tell us -- or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know sufficient facts. But if we use another minute for explanations, some of the companies also hired sportsmen, people who were able to move around quickly and, for example, Mr. Safranic, Sokol Safranic, which was the name of the firm was one of the owners, and he was a friend and a business colleague of Mr. Cermak. I remember him, because he was present in the public in connection with some sports events. But, as I say, there was a number of these firms, and, as the president of the Executive Council, we engaged another security firm which secured a number of public buildings in the city. But if you asked me about the management or the structure of ownership now, it would be too difficult for me to, try exactly after two decades, to answer this. However, there are clear records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that Mr. Cermak himself, apparently in the interview, is reported to have said that he had his 800 men doesn't refresh any of your memory as that Mr. Cermak may not have been only friendly or may have done business with such firms but that he might have been involved in ownership or management for those firms?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: As for the ownership issues, I repeat again, we might refer to official documents. As for the text, as far as I know, Mr. Cermak, he did not authorise the interviews he had given. If he had, probably the formulation would have been more precise. We have spent a lot of time on this, but this was an informal, colloquial, and quite imprecise statement, especially as regards the facts that were necessary to write anything like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you attend the interview?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of the interview having been recorded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: It probably was, because this is the way how one turns it into a text. However, when we do interviews, very often, then we make something more precise, when we -- we explain when we want to read through the statement that we gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But whether the written version reflects exactly, or less exactly, or not at all what Mr. Cermak said, you were not in a position to verify, did you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions of the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one matter arising from Your Honours' questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sometimes we don't know what's important or not to the Trial Chamber. Further Re-examination by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sokol Safranic was a name you mentioned, in fact, in answer to questions from Mr. Waespi. You've just mentioned that name in answer to questions from His Honour. Can you give an explanation by what you mean about Sokol Safranic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Sokol Safranic, at that time, was the name of a security firm. Mr. Safranic was either a part of the management or the owner of the company. Sokol was an old tradition name he used, and - with the hyphen in between - he added the last name of Safranic, the person who was either in the management or owned the firm itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does "Sokol" mean. What does that stand for? You said it was an old name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: It's an old Croatian historical name, which, indirectly associated to -- well, it is actually the name of a bird and also the name of an old sports association which existed throughout Croatian history.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Sokol means falcon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Cermak's connection, if any, with this firm? Can you explain that, why you mentioned this name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VEDRIS
utterances.text: Sorry ... I think he was on friendly terms with him. And they had some business contacts, which did not have to do with the security firm alone. Let us not forget that prior to 1991, Mr. Cermak had been a private entrepreneur and he had cooperated with a number of companies in different areas, although I have no particular knowledge of that. I told you that I only met him in the period following the first democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the questions by the Chamber were not aiming at further establishing the specifics of a relationship with one firm or another. It was -- to some extent it was also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- testing credibility and reliability which was at the foreground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I was trying to establish what the witness knew about it, obviously, because I've had instructions, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I inform you that the Chamber doesn't, at this moment, consider that it will be assisted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by -- by hearing or knowing more about the details of this one specific business relationship of -- with a firm the witness -- or a person the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I rise because there is one issue that I intend to bar table a document in response to a question or a line of questioning that was pursued by Mr. Waespi. I simply didn't have it at my disposal when Mr. Waespi concluded his examination. I will bar table it, but it is -- these are excerpts from the Martic OTP final trial brief concerning the questioning by Mr. Waespi at pages 53, lines 14 to 16. I'm willing to bar table it, but I wanted to let the Chamber know that I wanted to put those excerpts now in in response to that, in case the Chamber wanted me to put any of it to this witness who would have been present. The excerpts deals with the HDZ in 1990, 1991, and 1989. He has personal knowledge of it, but I'm content to bar table it. However the Chamber wishes to proceed. It is Exhibit 65 ter 1D114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber, at this moment, has no clear view on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but -- I don't know how many page it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's three paragraphs, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three paragraphs. Mr. Waespi, would you object to a bar table admission of the excerpts from the Martic final trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can exhibit something else in exchange, I wouldn't oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Come up with a proposal, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't object. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have that MFI'd, and I will only upload -- right now, the entire brief is in e-court, but we will shorten it. It is 65 ter 1D114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue seems not to be, at this moment, admission. The issue seems, rather, to be whether there would be any need to ask further questions to this witness about that. So, therefore, the Chamber would appreciate to have the relevant three paragraphs on the screen so that we can form an opinion as to whether we should keep the witness for a while or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, it is 65 ter 1D114, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The paragraphs were, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They're all yellow highlighted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All yellow highlighted. And the first one, 25 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then 31 and 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. If you would just first give us an opportunity to read 25. Could we -- I'm looking at my colleagues. Could we move on to the next page, to finish reading 25. Could we move to the next paragraph which was -- 32, you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 31 and 32, please. Could we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I take it that the relevance of tendering this as a bar table document is in relation to the -- the question put by Mr. Waespi? Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To put it short, it takes two to tango. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, it was the question on page 53 beginning at line 14 through 16 that President Tudjman made many moves which simply were to antagonise the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there is any need to put further questions to the witness in this respect. And the Chamber -- Mr. Waespi, you did not object to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the only issue is whether the witness was a party member and from when to when. I'm not sure that's part of his evidence. It's kind of related, but since this comes in while the witness is here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any problem by the other parties to hear from the witness whether he was a party member, HDZ, and from when to when?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vedris, last question to you: Were you a member of the HDZ, when did you become a party, if at all, and up until what moment were you a member? Yes, and I should have said "When did you become a party member," rather than to become a party. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a member of the Croatian Democratic Union as of the fall of 1990 until May 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then this -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I might have overstepped my ground. But if the witness could be asked why he left the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, if we are interested to know whether he was a member of the party, of course, if -- in the middle of a -- of a period in which -- politics is very important. If you leave a party, then it might be good to know, also, whether there was any specific reason why he left the party. Mr. Vedris, any specific reason why you left the party in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was. It was a personal reason of mine, as well as a reason of a number of then members of the HDZ and parliament. We believed that in the next stage that Croatia was embarking upon it was necessary to make more room for democracy and decision-making concerning the important issues that were raised within the HDZ itself. We tried to encourage such debates up to a point while we still believed that a dialogue of that kind may result in quality, the quality of the party, as well as the -- the quality of the wider context in which it worked. At the point in time when we assessed that it was difficult for us to expect to see that within the rather strict party framework, we decided to leave the party and terminate our membership in the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions -- and let's be open, more specifically, the last answer, has triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. But if I could just ask for an exhibit or -- I tender 65 ter 1D114. I don't know how the Chamber wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being the three paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The highlighted paragraphs from the Martic Prosecution's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Final brief. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Where there is no further need for the parties, as I understand, to put additional questions to the witness, Mr. Vedris, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, were put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Kay, I take it that you would prefer to have the break now and then start examination-in-chief of the next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break. And I have the best intention to resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I call Nadan Vidosevic, please. Your Honour, while the witness is being collected, can we deal with a matter that started at the end of Friday' session concerning the murders in Brgud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document shown on Sanction has been uploaded as 2D180367. And we ask that an exhibit number be assigned to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 13th of September report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1774.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, although you did not deal with the witness, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would take me a bit of an intellectual -- some gymnastics, to even imagine. But we will just wait and hear from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vidosevic. Before you give evidence in this courtroom. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence inquire that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you by Mr. Usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidosevic. Please be seated. Mr. Vidosevic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vidosevic.

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vidosevic, if you look at the screen on your right, we are going to produce a statement on there that you gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we have 2D00723, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If could you look at this statement, which is in your own language, and identify whether it is the same time you gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement I gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that your signature on the first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there, in your own language, is a date there, the 4th of May 2009 and your signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before signing this document, did you read through it to check that its contents were correct?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And the contents are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is the information in there, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the information is absolutely true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I was to ask you, today, the same questions that caused the answers that enabled this statement to be produced, would you give the same answers to those questions, if asked them in court today?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers as I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement is signed on the intervening pages, and I ask that this document, with the Court's leave, becomes an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The OTP has already responded that it does not object admission. Therefore, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will now make a short statement summarizing the contents of this statement, Mr. Vidosevic, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave, may I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vidosevic was born in 1960 in Split and graduated from the university in Split. In 1990, he was the general manager of the Dalmacija cement enterprise, and in March 1993, he was elected as a deputy of the Split-Dalmatia county, in the house of counties in the Sabor, the parliament, of the Republic of Croatia. And was the county prefect for Split-Dalmatia county. On the 12th of October, 1993, he was appointed as minister of the economy in the Government the Republic of Croatia and remained in that position until 18th September, 1995. And after that date, he became the president of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce, which is the position that he currently holds today. Your Honour, I'm just looking at paragraph 2 of the statement, and I notice the second paragraph has a typographic error and it should be September "1993," not September "1995," which flows from the information given in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we see that already in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vidosevic, as the minister of the economy, was aware of the vital significance, after the liberation of Knin, of the whole region that was now formally coming under the government of the Republic of Croatia, the importance of the liberated territories and their significance to the economy of Croatia at the time in August 1995. He was responsible for the operation of various state-owned enterprises, as they were at that time, and it was important for him to establish supplies of energy, being electricity, gas, and fuel, with the objective of factories within the region could resume working as soon as possible. He was the superior of a man called Zdenko Rincic, whom he appointed as the coordinator for the Ministry of Economy in Knin, and his tasks were to establish co-ordination with other institutions in Knin, to help establish normal life and conditions and start the economic recovery in Knin as soon as possible. And Mr. Rincic reported to him on the progress of the restoration of factories and other services as the time and days passed after the liberation of Knin. Mr. Vidosevic was aware that Mr. Rincic was using the support of Mr. Cermak, whom he was aware of, as having a man of great business experience and who was assisting in the normalisation of life in Knin and reestablishment of the utilities and infrastructure. And three days after Operation Storm had ended, he visited Knin with the prime minister and some other ministers to assess the situation in the town. On the 7th of September, 1995, he attended the special session of the government that was held in the fortress in Knin, where the government discussed and considered measures undertaken for the economic recovery in the region. Your Honour, that's a brief summary of the content of the statement. And with the Court's leave, I would like to ask Mr. Vidosevic a few extra questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware that it may be difficult, but I would invite the parties, still, to consider the possibility of concluding the testimony today. I have no assessments yet from the other Defence team nor from the Prosecution, so it's difficult for me to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi and I have collaborated on the matter and believe that this is a distinct possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it is not contradicted by parties with whom you also may have collaborated, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We neither, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vidosevic, a few questions concerning the nature of your evidence. August 1995, as minister of the economy, how would you have assessed, at that time, the economic state of the Republic of Croatia, before the liberation of Knin?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would assess it as very complex in every aspect. The 30 per cent of the territory was occupied. All the central roads were occupied. Three Adriatic ports, Split, Zadar, and Sibenik, were blocked. As for the network of roads, that was also threatened and so was the pipeline. We had a frontline in the norther part of the country as well, so the situation was very difficult. We had around 15 per cent of the population as refugees of which one third were refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we look at the Netherlands today, the equivalent would be if we had a million half and half people not living in their homes. It's something unthinkable. So under these conditions, we were fighting a very difficult battle to keep the Croatian economic system operating. And Knin was very important, and it would open a new vista. You can imagine how many millions we lost when transporting goods that had to be transported through the only road that we had that was across the bridge for Pag and then by ferry to the ground and then avoiding the front lines so that we could communicate with the rest of the world. I'm talking about the southern part of Croatia. We also had great problems with power supply, due to the very complex situation in Bosnia. Dalmatia was completely isolated, and that was one of the greatest challenges. We had problems with supplies. We had power cuts that was from 10 to 15 hours when the supply was impossible. Also, supply of food for the population. And therefore Knin was certainly the crucial point for the normal functioning of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vidosevic, if you take a breath now and then, our interpreters can also take a breath. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidosevic. Knin, then, was liberated on the 5th of August, 1995. And how important was it to get the region back to normality and stabilised for the Croatian economy?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just as I said, the costs that the state had were reduced several times. The life could become normal, and the state could function properly again, not only in this region. Not only the county of Knin and Zadar - today it is the county of Zadar and Sibenik - I don't mean just that region but also the entire territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what were the significant businesses in the Knin region that required getting back into operation as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were several, primarily this was the railway note [as interpreted]. Before the war, 3.000 employees worked at the railway junction in Knin. In addition to this, it was important to make the power supply system operational. It was part of the then-Yugoslav power supply system, Nikola Tesla. It was of exceptional importance for us. It was also necessary to provide regular oil and gas supplies. And what was also a challenge was to how to revive the companies. It was surprising for me that these companies were in an excellent condition when I visited Knin several days after the conclusion of operations, how one would make them operative again. Some of them were very perspective, and they could find a place on the market. Some were also in a good condition technically and technologically, but the demands of the market were not such that this was needed. I mean, not just the market in Croatia in mid-1990s but also in a broader context. So the challenge was how to find professionals and how to re-establish everything. What was exceptionally good was general enthusiasm of the people in the companies which were mainly publicly owned companies, such as the power supply system and the water supply system, but also other enterprises that were willing to assist. So that it was not a problem to motivate people; a bigger problem was to co-ordinate them so that the tasks would be carried out as soon as possible. And I believe that we managed to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How prepared was the government on the 5th of August, 1995, to start this process of taking over these industries and factories? Had there been any plan that had been prearranged, or was it something that was developed from the moment of liberation?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: We did not have any special plan, in case of liberation. Of course, we had experience from the war years, but we did not have a special plan. However, when things happened as they did, we were all happy that the possibility to start operating appeared. And, let me say that we demonstrated a high level of efficiency under relatively difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, in relation to his role in this, from what you were able to observe and learn, what was Mr. Cermak's role in relation to the matters that you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was crucial, and it was excellent. As an experienced businessman with some political experience; namely, he was the minister of economy before me, and he was the crucial person who made sure that the process would develop the way we wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidosevic. We are attempting to finish your evidence in one day, which I know will be important to you. And I have no further questions. But please wait there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Since the Gotovina and Markac Defence have informed the Chamber that they they've no questions for the witness. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Vidosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Mr. Vidosevic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vidosevic.

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First I'd like to turn to paragraph 4 of your witness statement, which is now D1775.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There you state that: "I did not know that Operation Oluja was going to start; I heard that the operation had started from the media, like all other citizens." Now, is it, therefore, fair to say that you weren't part of the inner circle of the Croatian structure that made these big decisions about whether to go to war or not?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to answer. When you are a minister in the government, then you are a member of the leading structures of your country. But the fact that the war operation would start was not part of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also weren't part of any of the meetings prior to 1995 that proceeded [sic] the launch of Operation Storm in which, you know, military issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the military sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it's no surprise that you were not involved, or knew of any plans, if there had been, in relation to the Serbs in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't quite put it that way. We had regular government meetings, and what was characteristic for the sessions of the Croatian governments in general was that decisions were always, without exception, made by consensus. So if any of the ministers did not agree with any of the proposed government decisions, then this item would be removed from the agenda. And on the basis of this, I can conclude that, if there was anything that was happening and that was directed against the Croatian citizens of Serbian ethnicity, it would not be accepted by the government, not just myself, but many of my colleagues. We would probably have left the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to paragraph 5 in your testimony. And you talked about that in chief as well. That was the transfer of Mr. Rincic, who was your deputy for special-purpose manufacturing industry and you appointed him as the economic coordinator. Now, was that a civilian or military activity that Mr. Rincic performed?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: He had civilian responsibilities as my assistant for a special-purpose manufacturing industry. And when Operation Storm was launched, he asked me to join the brigade that he had been a member of earlier, the 112th Brigade which covered the Zadar area, and I approved that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But when you appointed him as economic coordinator, was that a military role or a civilian role?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was a strictly civilian position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we come back to that in a second. But in paragraph 6 and also paragraph 5 and 9 you say that Mr. Rincic verbally reported to you on his activities by telephone. Now, when was that, that Mr. Rincic phoned you?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you are asking me about exact times, it is very difficult to say, because many years have passed. But, generally speaking, I can tell you that he reported to me about the issues which were interesting for me. And while responding to Mr. Kay, I explained a while ago what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was it the first time that Mr. Rincic reported back to you on his activities and the progress of the economic situation in Knin, as you point out in paragraph 6 of your statement? If you recall, after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not remember the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that was, you know, in those days following his appointment as coordinator in Knin, I take it?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was certainly after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Rincic when he phoned you? Was he in Knin?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was in Knin, but I know that he was active in a wider area, because we were also interested, for example, in the Knin Gips factory in Kosovo Polje, which is a bit further away of Knin in the direction of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know which phone he used when he reported back to you?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell that you. That is to say, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 9 of your statement you say that Mr. Rincic also reported to you about his cooperation with Mr. Cermak and Mr. Pasic. Now, what did he, Mr. Rincic, report to you about his cooperation with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: He reported to me, as I said earlier, about the things that I was interested in. And what I can say, I know this quite well because the instructions were quite precise, that he should put himself at the disposal of Mr. Cermak so that we could more easily fulfil our tasks, as Mr. Cermak was a very competent person who could help to resolve these very complex issues much supply and revival of economy, the supply of population and the recovery of economy in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that that was a civilian activity performed by Mr. Rincic. Now, did you know that he was performing these activities, at least when he left his office, in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you know that he was signing documents on behalf of Mr. Cermak, using the official letterhead and, indeed, the stamp of the Knin Garrison command?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on. Much later. But I must admit that this did not strike me as strange in any way because I know that both he and Mr. Cermak had an insufficient number of men for fulfilling their tasks, so if they had to have an exchange of tasks in a formal way, it seemed to me quite acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you would accept that Mr. Rincic was performing tasking on behalf of General Cermak, within the organisation of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible; but I would say, as part of their joint task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you also know that Mr. Rincic, sometimes intentionally, gave the impression that he was General Cermak's assistant or deputy?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but ... I could easily answer that. At the time, for the system which was being rebuilt to operate, it was very important to be efficient. And I suppose that Mr. Rincic then pragmatically, never thinking that today here in The Hague we would be discussing that, he would use the authority of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it was important, during those days, to be pragmatic?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also say in paragraph 10 of your witness statement that, on the basis of the reports you were getting from Mr. Rincic, you were: "... sure that Mr. Cermak was doing his job well." And you also met with Mr. Cermak at that time. Now, how many times did you meet with Mr. Cermak at that time, meaning during the time Mr. Cermak was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Several times, but these meetings were neither long nor very detailed because there was no need for such meetings. Things were happening at a pace that we wished to have. Everything was developing well. And Mr. Rincic was, in my view, an adequate link between the work that Mr. Cermak was doing and the area of work that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we heard, and I quoted you, that you thought that Mr. Cermak was doing his job well, based on the information received from Mr. Rincic. Now, in your conversations with Mr. Cermak, did you also get the impression that Mr. Cermak was doing his job well? Yes.

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Cermak as an entrepreneur from earlier times. He had two basic traits: one was extreme efficiency, and another, which was very important under the circumstances, was his degree of reliability. Hence, our discussions were short, effective, and I knew that what he said would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did anything apart from what you just told us stick out from these discussions between you and Mr. Cermak during that relevant period of time in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: Save for some courtesy discussions we had, there is nothing else that sticks out in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So he wouldn't have told you that his authority was ever questioned by, you know, his subordinates or by other units or -- or member of units, whether civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: NADAN VIDOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not under the impression that his authority was questioned in any way. There was, though, a general feeling that he and his associates had a lot of work to do. We were short of people, especially those qualified, and this one of the greatest challenges we faced, to come up with quality people who would be able to take on this enormous responsibility of normalizing life in Knin and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if we quickly could turn into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar could we turn into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Waespi, this concluded your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vidosevic, since the Chamber has no further questions for you either, this concludes your testimony in this court. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Chamber, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we would have 15 minutes left, but I can't imagine -- I don't know whether your next witness is available already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not in the building, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in the building. Then it would certainly take us more than 17 minutes to get him in here. So, under those circumstances, it would be wiser to allow you to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. I don't know if there's any housekeeping matters we need attend to in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic nods yes, so ... if we can use our time, then, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Over the weekend we e-mailed to the parties and the Chamber an agreement between the Prosecution and the Gotovina Defence with respect to P71. It is an additional page that was illegible in the original copies. Both the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution have inspected the original in the archive in Croatia and have come to an agreement as to what the text says. A translation has been prepared by CLSS, and we would ask the Chamber's leave to upload that one page into Exhibit P71. And the exhibit in English is ID 1D724999, and the B/C/S version is 1D724998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, P71 doesn't immediately ring a bell. What kind much document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the Split Military District operational diary. There was a page in there; we can call it up, if the Chamber wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just -- if the parties agree on a legible version of that page and earlier -- of course, I now -- of course, that rings a bell what document we are talking about. There were good reasons to have it admitted into evidence. So therefore, with the agreement of parties, to have a better copy in evidence which is always preferable seems to be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the page which was illegible, which is now added.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. And just for the record and so the Chamber is aware of the relevance, it's a page from a 9 August meeting where General Gotovina orders videotaping and photographing of perpetrators of -- of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber follows the parties in this respect and allows the addition to be uploaded and to be part of P71. Any other procedural matter? If not, we'll adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 3rd of November, 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
